names.c13-corner-girl: the girl from the corner house

pages.text: All night long, the winter wind blew round the village. It howled in the chimneys and rattled the shutters. Branches knocked against the roofs. Diana lay in bed and listened, with her blanket pulled up to her nose. At last, very late, the wind grew tired, and the village went quiet.

pages.text: In the morning, the sky was clean and pale. Diana looked out of her window. The street was covered in branches, big ones and small ones, and puddles shone everywhere. At the far end stood the little kindergarten. And right across its gate lay a huge branch from the old pine tree.
pages.speech: In the morning, the sky was clean and pale. Diana looked out of her window. The street was covered in branches, big ones and small ones, and puddles shone everywhere. At the far end stood the little kindergarten. And right across its gate lay a huge branch from the old pine tree.

pages.text: The little ones were already there in their raincoats, waiting with their teacher. The teacher took hold of the branch and pulled with all her might. The branch did not move. The little ones could not get in. One of them began to cry.

pages.text: Diana pulled on her boots and ran down the street. “Let me try!” She pushed the branch with both hands. She pushed with her shoulder. She pushed until her face went red. The branch did not move, not even a wiggle. “It’s too big for one,” said the teacher.
pages.speech: Diana pulled on her boots and ran down the street. “Let me try!” She pushed the branch with both hands. She pushed with her shoulder. She pushed until her face went red. The branch did not move, not even a wiggle. “It’s too big for one,” said the teacher.

pages.text: Diana stood still and thought. Too big for one. But what about more than one? She ran to the house with the blue door and knocked. Out came the twins, in matching boots, with matching sleepy faces. “Come and help,” said Diana. “The little ones can’t get in.”
pages.speech: Diana stood still and thought. Too big for one. But what about more than one? She ran to the house with the blue door and knocked. Out came the twins, in matching boots, with matching sleepy faces. “Come and help,” said Diana. “The little ones can’t get in.”

pages.text: Next she knocked at the back door of the bakery. Out came the baker’s boy, still holding his broom. Last of all, the girl from the corner house rolled down her ramp in her wheelchair, zipping up her coat. “I saw everything from my window,” she said. “I’m coming too.”
pages.speech: Next she knocked at the back door of the bakery. Out came the baker’s boy, still holding his broom. Last of all, the girl from the corner house rolled down her ramp in her wheelchair, zipping up her coat. “I saw everything from my window,” she said. “I’m coming too.”

pages.text: Diana’s mother came out too. She did not touch the branch. First she looked up and down the street, and up at the wires between the poles. Not one wire was down, and the branch was far from the poles. “All clear,” she said. “I’ll take the heavy end, and you help.”
pages.speech: Diana’s mother came out too. She did not touch the branch. First she looked up and down the street, and up at the wires between the poles. Not one wire was down, and the branch was far from the poles. “All clear,” she said. “I’ll take the heavy end, and you help.”

pages.text: Five children and one mother, one branch. Diana’s mother took hold of the thick end. The twins pulled one way. The baker’s boy pushed the other way. Diana tugged at a twig. The branch rocked and creaked, and it stayed exactly where it was. “It’s no use,” puffed the twins, both at once.
pages.speech: Five children and one mother, one branch. Diana’s mother took hold of the thick end. The twins pulled one way. The baker’s boy pushed the other way. Diana tugged at a twig. The branch rocked and creaked, and it stayed exactly where it was. “It’s no use,” puffed the twins, both at once.

pages.text: “Stop,” said the girl from the corner house. Everybody stopped. “We’re all pulling different ways,” she said. “We have to lift together, at the same time.” She pointed. “Diana’s mum at the thick end. Twins in the middle. You two at the thin end. When I say three, everybody lifts.”

pages.text: They took their places and bent their knees. Behind the fence, the little ones held their breath. “One, two, three, lift!” called the girl from the corner house. Diana’s mother and four pairs of small hands lifted together. And the huge branch rose off the ground, just a little, and moved.

Diana’s mother and four pairs of small hands lifted together. And the huge branch rose off the ground, just a little, and moved.

pages.text: “One, two, three, lift!” Step by step, they carried the branch to the side of the road and laid it on the grass. Diana’s arms ached, and the twins were laughing. Behind the fence, the little ones cheered so loudly that a cat jumped off a wall.
pages.speech: “One, two, three, lift!” Step by step, they carried the branch to the side of the road and laid it on the grass. Diana’s arms ached, and the twins were laughing. Behind the fence, the little ones cheered so loudly that a cat jumped off a wall.

pages.text: Then everybody found a job. The twins stacked the small branches in a neat pile. The baker’s boy swept the path with his broom. The girl from the corner house gathered pine cones on her lap, for the little ones. And Diana put both hands on the kindergarten gate.
pages.speech: Then everybody found a job. The twins stacked the small branches in a neat pile. The baker’s boy swept the path with his broom. The girl from the corner house gathered pine cones on her lap, for the little ones. And Diana put both hands on the kindergarten gate.

pages.text: The gate swung wide open. In marched the little ones, one by one, in their bright raincoats, waving as they went. “Thank you, thank you, thank you,” said their teacher. She shook every helper’s hand, even the twins’ muddy ones.

pages.text: The next morning, Diana walked past the kindergarten on her way to school. On the gate hung five drawings, one for each helper. A boy with a broom. A girl in a wheelchair, calling out loud. Two boys in yellow boots, in two drawings that looked exactly the same. And a girl in a red coat, pushing with all her might. Diana smiled all the way to school.

activity.title: Thank-You Cards
activity.goal: Write a short message for a real reader.

steps.caption: Who helps everyone? Choose one helper.
Fold a sheet into a card.
Write thank you, and one more line.
Give it together, with a grown-up.

activity.safety: Deliver the card together with an adult. Give it only when the helper has stopped and is free, never to a driver in traffic. If there is an accident, call your local emergency number.
activity.forAdult: In the story, Diana notices that the little ones cannot get into their kindergarten and gathers four other children to help. Nobody asked them, and the little ones thank them with drawings. This activity turns the thank-you round: the child notices the people who help everyone, every day, and writes to one of them. Helping people in need and taking part in a group are among the goals the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists for children of six to eight. Start by looking around together: who keeps the street clean, who drives the bus, who helps children cross, who cares for people in the clinic? Let the child choose one real person they can actually meet. Fold a sheet of paper into a card. On the front, the child draws the helper at work. Inside, they write “Thank you” and one more line of their own, such as “Our street is clean because of you.” Help with spelling only if asked; the message matters more than the spelling. Before delivering it, ask: how do you think they will feel when they read it? Then give it together, at a moment when the helper is free. Praise the noticing and the effort (“you saw who helps us”), not perfect writing. To make it easier, the child draws and says the words, and the adult writes them down. To make it harder, write a card for a helper the child has never thanked before, or make one card for each helper in a single morning.
activity.inClass: Each group of four chooses one helper of the school: the cleaner, the guard at the gate, the secretary or the cook. Each child makes a card, and the group delivers its cards together, with the teacher, at a quiet moment in that helper’s day. Afterwards the class talks about how the helper looked when they read them.
